notes.body:
Notice what the Imam does here: he takes three faults that look nothing alike and shows us they all grow from **a single hidden root**. That root is سوء الظن — thinking badly of Allah, quietly suspecting that He will not come through for us. Once that suspicion settles into a heart, it branches.

Watch how the same distrust feeds each fault in its own way:

- The miser clings to his wealth because, deep down, he does not believe Allah will replace what he gives away — so he clutches his money as a lifeline rather than a gift held on loan.
- The coward shrinks back because he does not trust that his safety and the very hour of his death rest in Allah's hand alone — so he comes to fear people the way he should fear only his Lord.
- The greedy man grasps for more because he cannot rest in the portion Allah has already measured out to him, forever convinced there will not be enough.

The single thread: each of these people has quietly decided that **Allah's provision, protection, and sufficiency cannot be relied upon** — and so each one reaches out with his own hand to seize what faith would have gladly entrusted to Allah.

That is why the Imam warns Malik so sharply against seating such a man near him. A ruler ringed by these three will be talked out of his generosity, frightened out of his courage, and flattered into mistaking his own selfishness for justice — because every one of them is pleading from the same despair: that Allah is not enough. So the cure is not three separate medicines but one — حسن الظن, a beautiful opinion of Allah, a heart that finally rests in the certainty that the One who fashioned us will never abandon us.
notes.anchor: yet a single bad opinion of God unites them
notes.quote: yet a single bad opinion of God unites them
etymology: بخل (miserliness): from the root ب-خ-ل, to hold back and refuse what ought to be handed over. The word keeps that gesture of a closed, tightening grip — the hand that will not open even when giving is right and easy.

جبن (cowardice): from ج-ب-ن. The same letters give جُبْن, cheese, which is milk that curdles and stiffens — a vivid picture of the coward's resolve, which thickens and shrinks back instead of flowing forward when courage is needed.

حرص (greed): from ح-ر-ص, to crave and covet with a burning, restless intensity. Its older sense is to scrape or strip a surface bare — the greedy soul rakes at the world the same way, never leaving anything untaken, never satisfied that it has enough.

notes.body:
Malik. The Imam meant is the one to whom Malik owes his allegiance, and in that moment that Imam is **Maulana Ali himself**. He does not name himself; he lets the office speak instead of the man.

The sentence rests on three supports, the same three the Quran names later in this letter:

- الله, the source of all authority
- the Prophet, His Messenger
- أولي الأمر, those placed in authority

'O ye who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.'
An-Nisa 4:59

For an Ismaili, 'those in authority' never became a closed chapter of the past; it is **the living Imam of each age**, present with the community in one's own lifetime. So the letter teaches a lasting principle dressed in a single moment: a soldier's loyalty should rise from Allah, through the Prophet, to the Imam who guides him now — for Malik, that is Maulana Ali; for a believer today, the Imam of this time.

Picture a lantern lit from one flame and passed hand to hand down the years. The light Malik receives is the same light, only carried by the hand nearest him. To be sincere toward one's Imam is not to admire a name in a book but to stay faithful to guidance that is **living and near**.
notes.anchor: the most sincere toward God, the Prophet, and your Imam
notes.quote: the most sincere toward God, the Prophet, and your Imam
etymology: إمام (Imam): from the root أ-م-م, meaning to head toward or aim at something. The imam is the one set out in front, whom the community faces and follows, just as a traveller keeps his face turned toward his destination.

نصيحة (sincere counsel): from the root ن-ص-ح, carrying the sense of purity, of a thing free of anything foreign — honey clear of its wax was called ناصح. To be sincere toward someone is to give counsel purified of every private motive.

أولو الأمر (those in authority): from the root أ-م-ر, to command. They are the ones entrusted with the الأمر, the affair or command of the community, holding an authority that ultimately traces back to Allah.

notes.body:
When Maulana Ali tells Malik to follow the part of the Prophet's practice (سنة) that "unites rather than divides," he is handing him a test he can actually use. Not every report about what the Prophet did carries the same weight: some are agreed upon by the whole community, while others are contested, narrated by one faction against another, or bent to serve a quarrel. **The uniting practice is the one whose truth is settled and shared; the dividing practice is the one that has become a banner for one group against the rest.**

Think of it the way we hold a family memory. When every relative tells the same story of what a grandparent did, that memory binds us together and no one fights over it. But when a single cousin insists on a version no one else recalls, and uses it to claim something for himself, the very same "memory" now splits the room.

So how do we actually tell them apart? A practice unites when three things hold true:

- it is transmitted openly and continuously, held in common rather than by one party
- it agrees with what is already clear and decisive (محكم) in the Book of Allah
- it gathers people toward a shared truth instead of arming a dispute

The anchor that settles the matter is named in the very verse the Imam is quoting — the command to obey "those in charge among us" (اولی الامر), the living guidance carried through the family of the Prophet (اهل البیت), who keep his true practice whole.
An-Nisa 4:59

**Measured against that appointed authority, the uniting practice is the one that flows from it, and the dividing practice is the one that cannot.**
notes.anchor: that part of his Sunna which unites rather than that which divides
notes.quote: that part of his Sunna which unites rather than that which divides
etymology: سنة (practice): from the root س-ن-ن, whose verb means to shape and to make water run in a fixed channel. From it comes the sense of a path worn smooth by repeated treading, so a سنة is a way followed so often that it becomes the road everyone shares — which is why a common practice naturally unites.

محكم (clear and decisive): from the root ح-ك-م, whose oldest picture is a bridle that restrains a horse. To judge (حكم) is to rein in wrongdoing, so a محكم verse is one whose meaning is reined in so firmly that it cannot bolt loose into dispute.

تفرقة (division): from the root ف-ر-ق, to split or part two things. The same root yields فرقان, the criterion that parts truth from falsehood — but turned this way it names the splitting of one community into contending pieces.

اولی الامر (those in charge): built on امر, which means both a command and an affair to be managed. The phrase points to those who at once hold the command and carry responsibility for the community's affairs — here, the authority that resolves what divides.
